speakerBio: Diabetologist with a special interest in the older inpatient with diabetes, who runs the trust's HHS pathway and teaches that the osmolality, not the glucose, is the number to watch.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 78-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought in after his daughter found him drowsy and confused. Over the past ten days he has been "off colour" with a cough, drinking litres of squash and passing huge volumes of urine, becoming progressively vague. He is profoundly dry — sunken eyes, tenting skin, a systolic of 92 — and barely rousable. His glucose reads HI on the meter; the lab returns 52 mmol/L. But here is what makes this not DKA: his venous pH is 7.33, his bicarbonate is 20, and his blood ketones are only 0.4 mmol/L. His calculated osmolality is allowed 360 mOsm/kg. This is hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state — a different disease, with a different tempo and a different treatment, and a mortality several times that of DKA. Treat it like DKA and you will kill him. This is the session on getting HHS right.

1 · 🧬 Pathophysiology — why there is no ketosis

HHS and DKA sit on the same spectrum of insulin-deficient hyperglycaemic crisis, but they diverge on one hinge: how much insulin is left.

  • In HHS there is relative insulin sufficiency — enough residual insulin (typically in type 2 diabetes) to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis, but nowhere near enough to control the blood glucose.
  • Because ketogenesis is suppressed, there is minimal or no ketoacidosis — the pH stays near-normal and ketones stay low.
  • Unchecked hyperglycaemia therefore climbs to extreme levels, often > 30–40 mmol/L, far higher than typical DKA.
  • The relentless glucose drives a massive osmotic diuresis over days, producing profound dehydration — a total fluid deficit of 100–220 mL/kg, or 8–15 litres in an adult, far greater than in DKA.
  • Water loss concentrates the blood, so serum osmolality rises above 320 mOsm/kg — the defining feature — and it is this hyperosmolality, not acidosis, that produces the depressed conscious level.

The diagnostic triad of HHS

CriterionThreshold
HyperglycaemiaGlucose usually > 30 mmol/L (often 40–60)
HyperosmolalityCalculated osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg
Absence of significant ketoacidosispH > 7.3, bicarbonate > 15 mmol/L, ketones < 3 mmol/L

Calculated osmolality = 2 × Na⁺ + glucose + urea (all in mmol/L). Learn it — it is the number that governs the whole treatment.

DKA is an acid problem; HHS is a water problem. In HHS the danger is written in the osmolality, not the pH.
💡 Conscious level tracks osmolality

The depressed GCS in HHS correlates with the osmolality, not the glucose per se. A patient who is comatose with an osmolality of 340–360 has an osmolality-driven encephalopathy; if the conscious level does not match the osmolality (e.g. coma at 320), look for another cause — stroke, sepsis, sedatives — because HHS alone should not explain it.

2 · 👤 The typical patient — insidious, elderly, precipitated

HHS wears a recognisable face, and it is not the young type 1 patient of the DKA lecture:

  • Older, usually with type 2 diabetes — and in up to a third, diabetes is previously undiagnosed; HHS can be the presentation.
  • Insidious onset over days to weeks — unlike the hours-to-a-day tempo of DKA — with progressive polyuria, thirst, weakness and declining cognition, so the deficit accumulated is enormous by the time they present.
  • Almost always a precipitant: infection (pneumonia, UTI — the commonest), myocardial infarction or stroke, poor access to water (frailty, dementia, care-home residents who cannot reach a drink), high-dose steroids, thiazides, or newly-started medication.
  • Often multiple comorbidities — cardiac, renal — that make the fluid management a tightrope.
⚠️ Always hunt the precipitant

HHS in an older patient is a red flag for a serious underlying event. Two precipitants kill silently and must be actively excluded in every case: infection (send cultures, examine the chest and urine, and treat early) and myocardial infarction (which is frequently painless in elderly diabetics — get an ECG and troponin). Do not anchor on "just the sugar."

3 · 💧 Management principle 1 — FLUID is the mainstay

The single most important therapeutic intervention in HHS is fluid, not insulin. Rehydration alone will lower the glucose substantially (by dilution and by restoring renal perfusion so the kidney excretes glucose), it restores circulating volume, and it begins to correct the osmolality. But — and this is the crux — it must be given more cautiously and more slowly than in DKA.

  • Fluid of choice is 0.9% sodium chloride. Even though the patient is hypernatraemic once you correct for glucose, 0.9% saline is relatively hypotonic to their grossly hyperosmolar plasma and is the safe starting fluid.
  • Aim for a positive balance of 3–6 litres by 12 hours and replacement of the estimated deficit over 24–48 hours — a deliberately gentler ramp than DKA, because the brain has equilibrated to a high osmolality over days and cannot tolerate rapid correction.
  • Only switch toward 0.45% saline if the osmolality is not declining despite adequate positive balance and the corrected sodium is rising.
  • Monitor the sodium and osmolality closely: as glucose falls, measured sodium will rise (glucose no longer holding water in the vessel) — a rise in sodium is expected and acceptable as long as osmolality is falling.
In HHS, fluid is the treatment and insulin is the assistant. Fix the water first.

4 · 💉 Management principle 2 — insulin LOW and LATE

This is the biggest single difference from DKA, and where teams trained on DKA do the most harm. In DKA you start fixed-rate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h immediately, because you must switch off ketogenesis. In HHS there is little or no ketogenesis to switch off, so insulin's only job is to help lower glucose — and fluid is already doing that.

  • Do NOT start insulin at the outset in most cases. Give fluid alone first and watch the glucose fall.
  • Start low-dose fixed-rate insulin at 0.05 units/kg/h (half the DKA rate) only if:
    • there is significant ketonaemia (blood ketones > 1 mmol/L or a mixed DKA/HHS picture), or
    • the glucose is no longer falling by at least ~5 mmol/L/h with fluid alone.
  • If you start insulin before the patient is volume-replete, you drive glucose (and its osmotic water) rapidly out of the vascular space into cells — collapsing the circulating volume and dropping osmolality too fast, precipitating cardiovascular collapse and cerebral oedema.
💡 The order matters

DKA: insulin is the star, fluid supports it. HHS: fluid is the star, insulin is a cautious, low-dose, often-delayed assistant. Starting HHS "the DKA way" — full-dose insulin up front, on a still-empty tank — is one of the classic errors that turns a survivable HHS into a fatal one.

5 · 🐌 Management principle 3 — go slowly, protect the brain

Because the brain has adapted to weeks of hyperosmolality by generating intracellular "idiogenic osmoles," a rapid fall in plasma osmolality pulls water into brain cells and causes cerebral oedema; overly rapid sodium shifts risk osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis). The whole tempo of HHS is therefore deliberately slow:

ParameterTarget rateWhy
Glucose fall4–6 mmol/L per hour (no faster)Faster falls collapse osmolality and risk cerebral oedema
Osmolality fall3–8 mOsm/kg per hour, graduallyAllows the brain to keep pace and avoids fluid shifts
Sodium changeRise as glucose falls is expected; corrected Na⁺ should not fall > ~10 mmol/L per 24 hPrevents osmotic demyelination
Glucose targetKeep glucose 10–15 mmol/L in the first 24 h — do NOT normaliseAdd 5–10% glucose to fluids once glucose < 14 to hold it there

Unlike DKA, where the endpoint is resolution of the acidosis/ketosis, the HHS endpoint is normalisation of osmolality and clinical/cognitive recovery, which typically takes up to 72 hours — a much longer haul.

6 · 🩸 The other two killers — VTE and the feet

HHS carries a very high risk of complications beyond the metabolic derangement:

  • Venous thromboembolism. The combination of extreme hyperosmolality, dehydration, immobility and often underlying malignancy or infection makes HHS a markedly prothrombotic state — arterial and venous thrombosis (including MI, stroke, DVT/PE) are leading causes of death. All HHS patients should receive prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin unless contraindicated, and some guidelines advise considering it for the duration of admission given the sustained risk.
  • Foot protection. These are frail, immobile, often obtunded patients with neuropathy and vascular disease — at high risk of pressure ulceration and diabetic foot complications. Heel protection, regular repositioning and daily foot inspection are part of the HHS care bundle, not an afterthought.
💡 The HHS bundle beyond glucose

Fluids, cautious insulin, potassium, hourly monitoring — and prophylactic LMWH, foot/heel protection, treat the precipitant, and a low threshold for HDU/ICU. HHS mortality (historically 15–20%) is driven as much by thrombosis, sepsis and comorbidity as by the sugar.

7 · ⚖️ DKA vs HHS — the contrast table

FeatureDKAHHS
Typical patientYounger, type 1 (or ketosis-prone T2)Older, type 2, often undiagnosed
OnsetHours to ~1 dayDays to weeks (insidious)
Residual insulinAbsentRelative sufficiency (suppresses ketones)
GlucoseOften 20–35 mmol/LExtreme, often > 30–40 (up to 60)
Ketones≥ 3 mmol/L (heavy)< 3 mmol/L (minimal)
AcidosispH < 7.3, HCO₃ < 15pH > 7.3, HCO₃ > 15 (near-normal)
OsmolalityVariable, often normal> 320 mOsm/kg (defining)
Fluid deficit~100 mL/kg (5–7 L)100–220 mL/kg (8–15 L)
Mainstay of treatmentInsulin (0.1 u/kg/h) + fluidFluid first; insulin low (0.05 u/kg/h) & often delayed
Correction speedFaster; resolve acidosisSlow; glucose 4–6 mmol/L/h, osmolality gradual
EndpointResolution of ketoacidosis (<24 h)Normal osmolality & cognition (up to 72 h)
VTE prophylaxisStandardMandatory — very high thrombotic risk
MortalityLow (~1–2%)High (historically 15–20%)

8 · 🔀 The mixed DKA/HHS picture

Up to a third of hyperglycaemic emergencies do not read purely as one or the other: a patient can be hyperosmolar AND ketoacidotic — extreme glucose and high osmolality (HHS features) with significant ketonaemia and acidosis (DKA features). This happens in type 2 patients who have decompensated far enough to lose ketone suppression, or in prolonged DKA with severe dehydration. The rule for a mixed picture:

  • Treat the ketoacidosis component like DKA — you do need insulin (start at the higher 0.1 u/kg/h if significant ketosis) to switch off ketogenesis — while respecting the HHS fluid caution: slower correction, watch the osmolality, keep the glucose fall to ~4–6 mmol/L/h, and do not let the osmolality plummet.
  • Get senior/diabetes input early — the mixed picture is the highest-risk group.
A patient can be both. When ketones and osmolality are both high, use DKA-strength insulin but HHS-strength patience.

9 · 💀 M&M — the osmolality that fell off a cliff

⚠️ Morbidity & Mortality: "we treated it like a big DKA"

An 82-year-old care-home resident presented with a glucose of 58 mmol/L, sodium 158, calculated osmolality 375, pH 7.34 and ketones 0.5 — textbook HHS. The night team, reaching for the familiar DKA protocol, started full-rate insulin at 0.1 units/kg/h immediately alongside aggressive 1-litre/hour saline. Over the next four hours the glucose crashed from 58 to 19 mmol/L — a fall of nearly 10 mmol/L/h — and the calculated osmolality dropped by more than 40 mOsm/kg. She became more, not less, obtunded, developed a bradycardia, and on CT had established cerebral oedema; she died two days later. The review found two linked errors: insulin started too early and too fast (fluid alone would have lowered the glucose gently), and correction far too rapid for a brain that had adapted to weeks of hyperosmolality. HHS is not a big DKA. Fluid first, insulin low and late, and bring the osmolality down slowly.

10 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. HHS = extreme hyperglycaemia (>30–40) + osmolality >320 + minimal ketones/acidosis, in an older type 2 patient with an insidious, days-long onset.
  2. Relative insulin sufficiency suppresses ketogenesis but not hyperglycaemia — that is why there is no significant ketoacidosis.
  3. Fluid is the mainstay — given more cautiously and slowly than DKA; deficits are huge (8–15 L) but replaced over 24–48 h.
  4. Insulin is low and late — often none at first; start 0.05 u/kg/h only if ketonaemia is present or glucose stops falling with fluid.
  5. Go slowly: glucose down 4–6 mmol/L/h, osmolality gradually, keep glucose 10–15 in the first 24 h — to avoid cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination.
  6. Always hunt the precipitant — infection and (often painless) MI above all.
  7. VTE prophylaxis is mandatory; protect the feet and heels.
  8. Mixed DKA/HHS exists — use DKA-strength insulin but HHS-strength patience.
  9. HHS mortality is several times that of DKA — treat it like the distinct, high-stakes emergency it is.

moderatorQs.q: Why is there minimal or no ketoacidosis in HHS despite a glucose of 50 mmol/L, when a DKA patient with a glucose of 25 is profoundly acidotic?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The difference is the amount of residual insulin. HHS occurs typically in type 2 diabetes where there is relative insulin sufficiency — enough circulating insulin to suppress lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, but nowhere near enough to control the blood glucose. So fat is not broken down into ketoacids and the pH stays near-normal (pH > 7.3, bicarbonate > 15, ketones < 3 mmol/L), while the glucose climbs unchecked to extreme levels. In DKA there is essentially no insulin, so lipolysis and ketogenesis run riot and the patient becomes profoundly ketoacidotic even at a lower glucose. The practical consequence is enormous: because there is little ketogenesis to switch off in HHS, insulin is not the mainstay — fluid is — and insulin is given low-dose and often delayed.

moderatorQs.q: A patient has HHS with a corrected sodium of 158 and osmolality of 365. As you rehydrate, the measured sodium rises to 165. Is your treatment failing?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Not necessarily — a rising measured sodium is expected and often acceptable in HHS as long as the osmolality is falling. As glucose comes down, it stops holding water in the vascular compartment, so the sodium concentration rises; this can look alarming but the number that matters is the osmolality (2×Na + glucose + urea), which should be declining gradually (about 3–8 mOsm/kg/h). What you must avoid is the osmolality falling too fast or the corrected sodium dropping by more than ~10 mmol/L in 24 hours, which risks osmotic demyelination. If the osmolality is not falling despite an adequate positive fluid balance and the sodium is climbing, that is when you switch from 0.9% to 0.45% saline. So judge success by the osmolality trajectory and the patient's conscious level, not the isolated sodium.

moderatorQs.q: How do you decide when — if ever — to start insulin in HHS, and at what rate?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: In HHS you do not start insulin at the outset in most patients. Fluid alone lowers the glucose by dilution and restored renal perfusion, and starting insulin on a still-empty circulation drives glucose and its osmotic water into cells too fast, collapsing the circulating volume and dropping osmolality dangerously. You start low-dose fixed-rate insulin at 0.05 units/kg/h — half the DKA rate — only if there is significant ketonaemia (blood ketones > 1 mmol/L, i.e. a mixed picture) or if the glucose stops falling by at least about 5 mmol/L/h with fluid alone. The target is a gentle glucose fall of 4–6 mmol/L per hour, holding glucose at 10–15 mmol/L for the first 24 hours (adding 5–10% glucose to the fluids once it drops below 14) rather than normalising it.

audienceQs.q: How do I actually calculate the osmolality at the bedside and what number defines HHS?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Use the simple calculated formula: osmolality = 2 × sodium + glucose + urea, with everything in mmol/L. So a patient with Na⁺ 155, glucose 45 and urea 15 has a calculated osmolality of (2×155) + 45 + 15 = 370 mOsm/kg. HHS is defined by a calculated osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg together with marked hyperglycaemia (usually > 30 mmol/L) and the absence of significant ketoacidosis (pH > 7.3, bicarbonate > 15, ketones < 3 mmol/L). The osmolality is the number you track hourly to guide the pace of treatment, because the conscious level tracks the osmolality — if a patient is comatose but the osmolality is only mildly raised, look for another cause such as stroke or sepsis.

audienceQs.q: Why are we giving this HHS patient a blood-thinning injection when they're not clotting or bleeding — and why all the fuss about their feet?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because HHS is one of the most prothrombotic states in medicine: the extreme hyperosmolality, severe dehydration, immobility and often underlying infection or malignancy massively raise the risk of clots — DVT, pulmonary embolism, stroke and heart attack — which are among the leading causes of death in HHS. So unless there's a specific contraindication, every HHS patient gets prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin, sometimes continued for the whole admission. The feet matter because these are frail, often obtunded, immobile patients with neuropathy and poor circulation, so they're at high risk of pressure ulcers and diabetic foot damage — heel protection, regular repositioning and daily foot checks are a formal part of the HHS care bundle.

audienceQs.q: My patient has a glucose of 48, osmolality of 340, but also ketones of 4.2 and a pH of 7.15. Is this DKA or HHS, and how do I treat it?
audienceQs.answerHTML: This is a mixed DKA/HHS picture — they meet HHS criteria on glucose and osmolality but also have significant ketoacidosis. This is the highest-risk group and needs early senior/diabetes input. The rule is to treat the ketoacidosis like DKA but with HHS-level caution on fluids and correction rate: because there is genuine, heavy ketosis you do need insulin to switch it off — start fixed-rate insulin at the higher 0.1 units/kg/h — but you simultaneously respect the HHS constraints, keeping the glucose fall to about 4–6 mmol/L/h, bringing the osmolality down gradually, watching the sodium, and being cautious with fluid volumes given the comorbidities. Give the mandatory VTE prophylaxis and hunt hard for the precipitant. In short: DKA-strength insulin, HHS-strength patience.
